subject: SST
label: Grade 02
task: Meet the outcome of every unit in Grade 02 Social science, and keep one piece of evidence for each.
condition: A 36-week school year, 4 units, a teacher or guide, a learning book or device, and local examples in the local language first with English support.
standard: Each unit: at least 4 of 5 attempts correct, said or written, with one real example from home or school. Course pass: no unit at 'Not yet' after one retry, and a pass in SA1 and SA2.

modules.title: What is a school
modules.outcome: describe people, rules and places in a school and draw a school map
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'What is a school', taught in a way that is short, playful, with objects, pictures and talk. The target is clear: describe people, rules and places in a school and draw a school map. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.
points: Place it: find where and when 'What is a school' happens, on a map, a timeline or in a local example.
Gather: read or listen to two short sources and note who is speaking and why.
Use it: describe people, rules and places in a school and draw a school map. Give a reason and one piece of evidence for every point.
Weigh it: say what another person might think, and why, before you decide.
modules.example: Solved: List five places near you and who works there. Say how each helps the community and one way you can help. Method: Model run for 'What is a school'. Question: what happened, or what is the situation, and why? Sources: two short extracts, a map or table. Notes: who, what, where, when, why. Answer: three sentences, each with a reason and a piece of evidence. Check: is there a point of view that you have not considered? What a good answer looks like: facts are correct, reasons are linked to evidence, and one other point of view is named fairly.
modules.activity: About 20 to 30 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: one page in your learning book.
modules.standard: Describe people, rules and places in a school and draw a school map: at least 4 of 5 attempts correct, said or written, with one real example from home or school.
steps: Step 1, List the people and places in a school. People: principal, teachers, librarian, nurse, guard, cleaner, students. Places: classrooms, library, playground, canteen, office, clinic. Each person and place has a job that helps students learn and stay safe.

Step 2, Plan a simple map. Draw the main gate at the bottom of the page. Put the office to the right of the gate, the library straight ahead, the playground at the top, and Class 2B on the left. Number the places 1 to 4.

Step 3, Add a key. Square = classroom, star = library, tree = playground, triangle = office. A key explains the symbols so anyone can read the map. Without a key, a reader cannot tell a library from a canteen.

Step 4, Give directions from the gate. 'Walk straight to the library. Turn left and go past the library to reach Class 2B.' Use words like straight, left, right, near and far. Check by tracing the path with your finger.
Step 5, Explain two rules with reasons. 'We do not run on the stairs because we could fall.' 'We keep the library quiet so others can read.' A rule plus a reason makes a full answer.
Step 6, Your turn: tell how to go from the main gate to the playground on this map. Model answer: 'From the main gate, walk straight past the library to reach the playground at the top of the page.'

modules.title: Our neighbourhood and community
modules.outcome: describe community helpers and public places
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Our neighbourhood and community', taught in a way that is short, playful, with objects, pictures and talk. The target is clear: describe community helpers and public places. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.
points: Place it: find where and when 'Our neighbourhood and community' happens, on a map, a timeline or in a local example.
Gather: read or listen to two short sources and note who is speaking and why.
Use it: describe community helpers and public places. Give a reason and one piece of evidence for every point.
Weigh it: say what another person might think, and why, before you decide.
modules.example: Solved: List five places near you and who works there. Say how each helps the community and one way you can help. Method: Model run for 'Our neighbourhood and community'. Question: what happened, or what is the situation, and why? Sources: two short extracts, a map or table. Notes: who, what, where, when, why. Answer: three sentences, each with a reason and a piece of evidence. Check: is there a point of view that you have not considered? What a good answer looks like: facts are correct, reasons are linked to evidence, and one other point of view is named fairly.
modules.activity: About 20 to 30 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: one page in your learning book.
modules.standard: Describe community helpers and public places: at least 4 of 5 attempts correct, said or written, with one real example from home or school.
steps: Step 1, A community is a group of people who live near each other and share places and services. Our community has homes, shops, a park, a library and a clinic. People in a community depend on each other.

Step 2, Name community helpers and their tools. A nurse uses a thermometer, a police officer keeps roads safe, a bus driver drives children to school, and a street cleaner uses a broom and bin lorry. Write a line: 'A nurse helps sick people feel better.'

Step 3, Name public places and who may use them. The library lends books, the park is for play, the hospital treats the sick and the post office sends parcels. Public places belong to everyone, so we keep them clean and share them fairly.

Step 4, Think about a problem. What happens if the cleaner stops work for a week? Rubbish piles up, bad smells spread, flies come and people may get ill. This shows why every helper matters to the whole community.
Step 5, Write a model answer with a reason: 'The librarian helps us because she finds books and teaches us to take care of them. Without her, books would be lost and hard to find.'
Step 6, Your turn: choose one public place and say how to look after it. Model answer: 'In the park I put my rubbish in the bin and do not pick the flowers, so everyone can enjoy it.'

modules.title: The UAE: emirates and landmarks
modules.outcome: name the seven emirates and some landmarks
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'The UAE: emirates and landmarks', taught in a way that is short, playful, with objects, pictures and talk. The target is clear: name the seven emirates and some landmarks. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.
points: Place it: find where and when 'The UAE: emirates and landmarks' happens, on a map, a timeline or in a local example.
Gather: read or listen to two short sources and note who is speaking and why.
Use it: name the seven emirates and some landmarks. Give a reason and one piece of evidence for every point.
Weigh it: say what another person might think, and why, before you decide.
modules.example: Solved: The UAE has seven emirates: Abu Dhabi, Dubai, Sharjah, Ajman, Umm Al Quwain, Ras Al Khaimah and Fujairah. National Day is 2 December (1971). Name the capital and one landmark. Method: Model run for 'The UAE: emirates and landmarks'. Question: what happened, or what is the situation, and why? Sources: two short extracts, a map or table. Notes: who, what, where, when, why. Answer: three sentences, each with a reason and a piece of evidence. Check: is there a point of view that you have not considered? What a good answer looks like: facts are correct, reasons are linked to evidence, and one other point of view is named fairly.
modules.activity: About 20 to 30 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: one page in your learning book.
modules.standard: Name the seven emirates and some landmarks: at least 4 of 5 attempts correct, said or written, with one real example from home or school.
steps: Step 1, Name the seven emirates: Abu Dhabi, Dubai, Sharjah, Ajman, Umm Al Quwain, Ras Al Khaimah and Fujairah. Say them while clapping the syllables, then say them again with your eyes closed. Count them on your fingers: there are seven.

Step 2, Know two facts. Abu Dhabi is the capital and the largest emirate, with more land than the other six together. Ajman is the smallest emirate. Fujairah is on the east coast by the Gulf of Oman, and the other emirates lie mostly along the Arabian Gulf.

Step 3, Match landmarks to emirates. Burj Khalifa in Dubai is the tallest building, 828 m high. Qasr Al Hosn is an old fort in Abu Dhabi city, and Al Jahili Fort is in Al Ain. Jebel Jais in Ras Al Khaimah is the highest mountain, 1,934 m. Fujairah and Umm Al Quwain each have an old fort too.

Step 4, Place the emirates on a map. Along the northern Gulf coast from west to east come Abu Dhabi, Dubai, Sharjah, Ajman, Umm Al Quwain and Ras Al Khaimah. Fujairah sits on the opposite, eastern coast. Colour each emirate a different colour and write its name.

Step 5, Play a matching game. Make seven cards with emirate names and seven cards with a landmark or a fact. Mix them and match: 'tallest building' goes with Dubai, 'highest mountain' with Ras Al Khaimah, 'capital city' with Abu Dhabi. Check your answers with a partner.
Step 6, Your turn: name the emirate with Burj Khalifa, and the emirate with Jebel Jais. How many emirates are there in all? Answer: Dubai, Ras Al Khaimah, and seven emirates in all.

modules.title: Needs and wants
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Needs and wants', taught in a way that is short, playful, with objects, pictures and talk. The target is clear: sort needs from wants. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.
points: Place it: find where and when 'Needs and wants' happens, on a map, a timeline or in a local example.
Gather: read or listen to two short sources and note who is speaking and why.
Use it: sort needs from wants. Give a reason and one piece of evidence for every point.
Weigh it: say what another person might think, and why, before you decide.
modules.example: Solved: Needs: food, water, shelter, clothes. Wants: a toy, a game. With 100 coins: spend 70 on needs and 30 on wants, and save any extra. Method: Model run for 'Needs and wants'. Question: what happened, or what is the situation, and why? Sources: two short extracts, a map or table. Notes: who, what, where, when, why. Answer: three sentences, each with a reason and a piece of evidence. Check: is there a point of view that you have not considered? What a good answer looks like: facts are correct, reasons are linked to evidence, and one other point of view is named fairly.
modules.activity: About 20 to 30 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: one page in your learning book.
modules.standard: Sort needs from wants: at least 4 of 5 attempts correct, said or written, with one real example from home or school.
steps: Step 1, Learn the two words. A need is something we must have to live and stay healthy: food, water, clothes, a home and medicine. A want is something nice to have but we can live without it: a toy, a game, a sweet.

Step 2, Sort eight items: rice, water bottle, toy car, winter jacket in a cold place, video game, medicine, ice cream, bicycle. Needs: rice, water bottle, jacket, medicine. Wants: toy car, video game, ice cream, bicycle.

Step 3, Check a tricky case. A school bag is a need because we carry books. A bag with a cartoon picture and lights is a want. So one thing can include both a need and a want. Ask, 'Could I live and learn without this part?'
Step 4, Make a choice. Maya's family can buy only one thing this week: a new football or healthy food for dinner. Food is a need, so it comes first. Wants can wait or be saved for.
Step 5, Write a model answer: 'Water is a need because our body cannot live without it. A tablet is a want because I can still learn and play without it.' Always give a reason.
Step 6, Your turn: is a coat a need or want in winter, and a toy robot? Model answer: 'A coat is a need because it keeps me warm. A toy robot is a want because I can live without it.'
